name: Guru Har Rai
summary: Born in 1630, Guru Har Rai led the Sikhs from the age of 14. He is remembered for gentleness, care for animals and plants, and healing, while keeping the Sikh community safe and peaceful.
about: Har Rai was born on 16 January 1630 in Kiratpur Sahib, in the foothills of the Himalayas. His grandfather, Guru Hargobind, named him the Guru, and he took the seat on 3 March 1644 at about 14 years old. Sikh tradition says Guru Hargobind advised him to put teaching ahead of fighting, so he kept the Sikh community's strength but avoided open war with the Mughals. Historians note he took the side of the prince Dara Shikoh in the Mughal succession quarrel, which later brought a summons from the winner, Aurangzeb. He sent his elder son Ram Rai to court, and when Ram Rai changed a line of scripture to please the emperor, Har Rai chose his younger son, Har Krishan, as the next Guru. He died at Kiratpur on 6 October 1661, aged 31. Some modern Sikhs call him the Green Guru for his care for nature, a name popularised by EcoSikh in 2013.
kidSummary: Guru Har Rai was a Sikh Guru who lived nearly 400 years ago. He was famous for being very gentle. He cared for animals and plants, and he shared healing herbs with people who were ill. Today many Sikhs remember him whenever they plant a tree.

story.title: A very young Guru
story.text: Guru Hargobind chose his grandson Har Rai as the next Guru. When Har Rai took the seat in 1644, he was only about fourteen years old.

story.title: A gentle heart
story.text: A traditional tale says that his cloak once brushed against a flower and broke its stem. He was so sad that he walked more carefully from then on, to keep every living thing safe.

story.title: Animals and herbs at Kiratpur
story.text: Sikh sources say he kept animals safe in a park and grew healing plants in a garden at Kiratpur. People who were sick came to him for medicine and kindness.

story.title: Helping a prince in need
story.text: A tradition says the Guru sent medicine to the Mughal prince Dara Shikoh when he was unwell. Later, the emperor Aurangzeb was unhappy with this help and called the Guru to explain himself.

story.title: A choice about honesty
story.text: Har Rai sent his son Ram Rai to the court instead. Ram Rai changed a line of scripture to please the emperor, so the Guru named his five-year-old son, Har Krishan, as the next Guru.

teaches: Be gentle with every living thing
Care for nature and heal others
Stay true to scripture even under pressure
texts: Guru Granth Sahib (one verse tentatively linked to him)

facts.text: Asked why he helped Dara Shikoh, whose ancestors had troubled the Gurus, he is believed to have replied that when one hand plucks flowers and gives them away, both hands keep the fragrance.
He became Guru on 3 March 1644 when he was only about 14, after his grandfather died. His own father had died when he was about 8, and he had been married at 10.
Sikh tradition tells of him as a boy becoming upset when his cloak accidentally snapped a flower off its stem, and he became more careful with his clothing afterward.
Traditional accounts say he hunted like earlier Gurus but never harmed the animals, instead keeping them safe in an animal park at Kiratpur.
Naulakha Bagh at Kiratpur, 'garden of 900,000 plants', is believed in Sikh tradition to have been founded and cared for by him, and it held many medicinal plants.

Sikh Environment Day is on 14 March; the date was chosen in 2011 to mark the anniversary of his guruship. In 2013 the president of EcoSikh described him as the 'green guru', stressing his close bond with nature.

In one tradition, Dara Shikoh was close to death from poison, possibly tiger whiskers, and nothing worked until a minister suggested the Guru's herb garden. Guru Har Rai freely sent healing plants, and the prince recovered.

Sikh sources say that when Dara Shikoh fled his brother's army, the Guru's soldiers held the crossing of the Beas so the prince could escape toward Lahore, though accounts differ on how far they fought.
Writers say he kept a standing cavalry of about 2,200 horsemen ready at all times, yet chose peace over fighting.

After Dara Shikoh lost to Aurangzeb in 1658 and was executed, Aurangzeb summoned Har Rai in 1660 to explain himself. The Guru sent his 13-year-old son Ram Rai, whom the emperor kept at court as a hostage.

Aurangzeb questioned Ram Rai about a verse in the Adi Granth that he said insulted Muslims, and Ram Rai changed its meaning to please him. His father cut him off and chose his five-year-old younger son, Har Krishan, as the next Guru.
Aurangzeb rewarded Ram Rai with land grants in the Dehra Dun region. Ram Rai set up his dera, or camp, in the dun, the valley, in 1676, and the city of Dehradun takes its name from that dera.

Refusing to back Ram Rai's claim, he is recorded as saying that guruship is like a tiger's milk, which can only be held in a golden cup, and that only someone ready to give their whole life to it is worthy.
Hargobind passed over his eldest grandson Dhir Mal, who had Mughal land grants and backing, and named Har Rai. The pattern repeated when Har Rai chose his second son instead of the eldest.

Soon after he took the seat, Mughal forces under Najabat Khan invaded the lands of Tara Chand of Hindur and captured him. Har Rai left Kiratpur for Thapal in Sirmur, where he gave his first teaching, and stayed out of the fight, following Hargobind's advice.

Later sources claimed he had seven or eight wives, but historians reject this. Ganda Singh notes the story survives only on unpaged leaves of one Suraj Prakash manuscript that look added, while older sources name one wife, Sulakhani or Kishan Kaur.

A short salok signed with his name sits in the Kiratpuri Bir of the Guru Granth Sahib, but historians say it cannot be securely attributed to him, since the Guru Miharban used the same signature line. Many Sikhs believe he left no bani.
A 2013 painting given to EcoSikh shows him handing a tree to a petitioner to plant, but the tree is a eucalyptus, a species not found in India in his lifetime.
Mughal records agree that he supported Dara Shikoh in the war of succession, and that he gave the prince medical care when he may have been poisoned by Mughal operatives.

Some masands led by his elder brother Dhir Mal, backed by Shah Jahan's land grants, tried to start a rival guruship. Har Rai kept Sikhs united partly by appointing new masands as heads of manjis, such as one for eastern India and one for Rajasthan.

quiz.q: How old was Har Rai when he became Guru?
quiz.why: He became Guru on 3 March 1644 when he was about 14 years old.

quiz.q: Why is Guru Har Rai sometimes called the Green Guru?
options: He loved plants, animals and healing
quiz.why: He is remembered for caring about plants, animals and healing herbs; EcoSikh used the name Green Guru in 2013.

quiz.q: Which son did Guru Har Rai choose as the next Guru?
quiz.why: He chose five-year-old Har Krishan after Ram Rai changed scripture for the emperor.

quiz.q: Where did Guru Har Rai keep the animals he hunted, without harming them?
options: In an animal park at Kiratpur
On the banks of the Beas
quiz.why: Traditional accounts say he hunted like earlier Gurus but never killed the animals, keeping them safe in an animal park at Kiratpur.

quiz.q: What did he say about the hand that plucks flowers and gives them away?
quiz.why: In Sikh tradition he used this saying to explain why he helped others, even those whose ancestors had troubled the Gurus.
